# Part 1 · The reasoning core — S1 to S7

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Section 2 — Arg, Prf, Err</div>
<div class="fs-title">Logic and proof — the whole of it</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Seven sessions. If you can reproduce these from memory you have the entire non-A-level content of Paper 2; everything else on the paper is Paper 1 mathematics wearing a logical wrapper.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### S1 · Statement forms ★

$$A\Rightarrow B\;=\;\text{“if }A\text{ then }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}A\text{ only if }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}B\text{ if }A\text{”}$$

**The bare "if" introduces the forcing statement.** So "$A$ **if** $B$" is $B\Rightarrow A$ — backwards from
the reading order.

"$A$ **if and only if** $B$" is both arrows: $A\Leftrightarrow B$.

**Reversed wording:** in "a condition **for** $Q$ is $P$", the target follows the word *for*. Find the
target first, then the condition.

[the trap: "only if" points forwards, "if" points backwards]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S2 · Converse and contrapositive ★

| | form | equivalent to the original? |
|---|---|---|
| statement | $A\Rightarrow B$ | — |
| **converse** | $B\Rightarrow A$ | **no** |
| inverse | $\lnot A\Rightarrow\lnot B$ | **no** |
| **contrapositive** | $\lnot B\Rightarrow\lnot A$ | **always yes** |

The inverse and the converse are contrapositives *of each other*, so they stand or fall together.

When a question asks **"which must be true"**, the answer is almost always the contrapositive and the
**converse is the trap option**.

**The standard question: "which is logically equivalent?"** You are being asked to find one of

$$\text{if }P\text{ then }Q
\ \ \equiv\ \ P\ \textbf{only if}\ Q
\ \ \equiv\ \ \lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P .$$

**Method: symbolise the whole sentence first, then swap and negate.** Write $P$ and $Q$ down as labels,
read the sentence into $P\Rightarrow Q$, then exchange the two sides **and** negate both. Never try to
rearrange the English directly.

[negate a compound with De Morgan — see S4]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S3 · Necessary and sufficient ★

$$\text{“}P\text{ sufficient for }Q\text{”}=P\Rightarrow Q\qquad
\text{“}P\text{ necessary for }Q\text{”}=Q\Rightarrow P$$

**Sufficient points forwards; necessary points backwards.**

**The routine that answers every one of these.** Write the *exact* set of cases making each statement
true, then compare by inclusion:

$$P\subset Q\Rightarrow\textbf{sufficient, not necessary}\qquad
Q\subset P\Rightarrow\textbf{necessary, not sufficient}$$
$$P=Q\Rightarrow\textbf{both}\qquad\text{overlapping}\Rightarrow\textbf{neither}$$

**The tip: turn every "necessary" into a "sufficient".** The two words describe the same arrow from opposite
ends, so

"$X$ is **necessary** for $Y$" &nbsp;=&nbsp; "$Y$ is **sufficient** for $X$".

Rewrite the question that way and you only ever have to think in **one** direction.

**Then: the sufficient one is always the more restricted condition — the smaller set.** Of the two, whichever
is **harder to satisfy** is sufficient for the other; the easier one is necessary.

[25 % of recent papers — the largest single block of marks]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4 · Quantifiers and negation ★

$$\lnot(\forall x,\;P)=\exists x,\;\lnot P\qquad\lnot(\exists x,\;P)=\forall x,\;\lnot P$$

The negation of "**all** X are Y" is "**some** X is **not** Y" — *not* "no X is Y".

**De Morgan.** $\lnot(P\text{ and }Q)=\lnot P\text{ or }\lnot Q$; $\lnot(P\text{ or }Q)=\lnot P\text{ and }\lnot Q$.

**Negating an implication.** $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P\text{ **and** }\lnot Q$ — never "if $P$ then not $Q$".

**Order matters.** $\forall x\,\exists y$ lets $y$ depend on $x$; $\exists y\,\forall x$ needs one $y$ for
all $x$ at once — far stronger.

[to negate a chain, flip every quantifier in order, then the inside]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S5 · Proof methods

- **Direct** — assume the hypothesis, deduce the conclusion. Represent generally ($2k$, $2k+1$).
- **By cases** — split by remainder; check every case.
- **By contradiction** — assume the negation, derive an absurdity.
- **By counterexample** — to disprove "for all", one case is enough.

**A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis *and* fail the conclusion.** A case where the hypothesis
fails proves nothing.

**"Possible" is $\exists$** — produce one witness. **"Must" is $\forall$** — one counterexample destroys it.

[read which one you were given before starting]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S6 · Scrambled proofs

Anchor the ends, then follow the dependencies.

1. **First line** introduces notation or assumes the hypothesis ("Let…", "Suppose…").
2. **Last line** states the conclusion, or the contradiction.
3. A line can only come after every line it **uses**.
4. Connecting words carry the order: *therefore*, *hence*, *so*, *it follows*.

**Build the chain yourself before reading the options** — the distractors are a tidy but wrong parallel
chain, so comparing them directly is slower and riskier.

[rare: one TMUA question in eight years, 2016 P2 Q7]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · The 20-second error scan ★

1. **Name the target:** write the claim as $P\Rightarrow Q$.
2. **Check the ends:** does the proof start from $P$ and reach $Q$ — or has it proved the converse?
3. **Read one arrow at a time:** ask, *"Does this follow for every value still allowed?"*
4. **Stop at the first false claim**, not the final absurdity it causes.
5. **Stress-test the boundary:** try $0$, $1$, equality, the smallest case, and any excluded endpoint.

Every line may be true but the **link** between two lines can still fail. A one-way step is not an error if
it is stated only as a necessary condition; the error comes when it is treated as reversible.

[do not force an error — sometimes the whole argument is valid]{.eg}
:::
::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · High-risk moves ★

| If you see… | Check immediately… |
|---|---|
| **cancel / divide** | Can the divisor be $0$? Factor and split cases instead. |
| **square / root** | Squaring may add roots; $\sqrt{u^2}=\lvert u\rvert$; check candidates in the original. |
| **inequality** | Is the sign known? Negative multipliers and decreasing functions reverse the sign; $0<a<1$ makes $\log_a$ decreasing. |
| **inverse or trig step** | Is the function one-to-one on the stated domain? $\sin A=\sin B\not\Rightarrow A=B$. |
| **theorem or implication** | Are all hypotheses met, and is the arrow being used in the stated direction? |
| **"for all" claim** | One valid counterexample destroys it; test exceptional and boundary cases. |

**Wording controls equivalence.** "Is equivalent to" demands both directions. "Any solution must satisfy"
claims only one direction; those values are **candidates**, not solutions, until checked.

[full notes: **[S7 concepts](../toolkit/s07_concepts.qmd)** · **[S7 extended](../toolkit/s07_extended_equivalence.qmd)**]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

## Equivalence, necessary and sufficient conditions {#s2-check}

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · One arrow or two?</div>
<div class="fs-title">Equivalent means exactly the same cases</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Track both the logical direction and the domain. A valid one-way step produces a necessary condition; it does not automatically produce an equivalent statement.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Equivalent = both directions

$$A\Leftrightarrow B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(A\Rightarrow B)\text{ and }(B\Rightarrow A).$$

Across the stated domain, $A$ and $B$ must be true in **exactly the same cases**. For equations or
inequalities, this means the **same solution set**: no gained solutions and no lost solutions.

| known | correct description |
|---|---|
| $A\Leftrightarrow B$ | each is necessary **and** sufficient for the other |
| $A\Rightarrow B$ only | $A$ is sufficient for $B$; $B$ is necessary for $A$ |
| $B\Rightarrow A$ only | $B$ is sufficient for $A$; $A$ is necessary for $B$ |

[tail = sufficient; head = necessary]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### A valid one-way step

Let $A:\sqrt{2x+3}=x$ and $B:2x+3=x^2$. Squaring proves

$$A\Rightarrow B,$$

so $B$ is **necessary for** $A$. But $x=-1$ satisfies $B$ and not $A$, so $B\not\Rightarrow A$.

The safe wording is:

> Any solution of $A$ **must satisfy** $B$; solve $B$, then check those candidates in $A$.

A one-way step can be valid. The error is calling it **equivalent**, or promoting unchecked candidates to
solutions.

[$A\Rightarrow B$ means $\operatorname{Sol}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}(B)$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Equivalent statement $\neq$ negation

For $S:\ \forall n>1,\ P(n)\Rightarrow Q(n)$:

| asked for | result |
|---|---|
| **equivalent to $S$** | $\forall n>1,\ \lnot Q(n)\Rightarrow\lnot P(n)$ |
| **negation of $S$** | $\exists n>1,\ P(n)\wedge\lnot Q(n)$ |

The first is the **contrapositive**, so it has the same truth conditions as $S$. The second gives exactly
the counterexample that makes $S$ false.

The domain restriction $n>1$ stays fixed; it is not replaced by $n\le1$.

[equivalent: same truth · negation: opposite truth]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

## Part 1 examples — high-frequency traps

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · S1–S7</div>
<div class="fs-title">Ten questions to check before the exam</div>
<div class="fs-sub">One question for each of S1–S7, plus three harder S4 checks from the dedicated clinic. Decide first; then read the check.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### S1 · Read the wording

Let $P$ mean “$n$ is divisible by $6$” and $Q$ mean “$n$ is divisible by $3$”. Which are equivalent to
$P\Rightarrow Q$?

1. $P$ **only if** $Q$.
2. $Q$ **if** $P$.
3. $P$ **if** $Q$.
4. $Q$ **only if** $P$.

**Check:** **1 and 2**. Statements 3 and 4 are the converse, $Q\Rightarrow P$; $n=3$ disproves it.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S2 · Equivalent or negated?

For every integer $n>1$,

$$n^2\text{ even}\Rightarrow n\text{ even}.$$

Write (a) an equivalent statement and (b) its negation.

**Check:** (a) the contrapositive: *if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd*. (b) there exists an integer $n>1$
such that $n^2$ is even **and** $n$ is odd.

[swap-and-negate gives an equivalent; keep-and-deny gives the negation]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S3 · Necessary means the larger set

For real $x$, let

$$A:x<2,\quad B:0<x<1,\quad C:x^2<1,$$
$$D:\lvert x-1\rvert<2,\quad E:x^2<4.$$

Which statement is necessary for **exactly three** of the other four?

**Check:** **$A$**. Its set $(-\infty,2)$ contains $B=(0,1)$, $C=(-1,1)$ and $E=(-2,2)$, but not
$D=(-1,3)$.

[Woonju dedicated clinic: draw the five intervals before counting]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4 · Quantifier order

Which statements are true?

1. $\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.
2. $\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \exists n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.
3. $\exists x\in\mathbb R\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z^+:\ x<n$.

**Check:** **2 and 3**. In 2, choose an $n$ depending on $x$. In 3, one value such as $x=0$ works for
every positive integer $n$. Statement 1 fails at $x=100,n=1$.

[2022 Paper 2 trap: later variables may depend on earlier ones]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Negate through an implication

Negate

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x:\quad
\lvert x-a\rvert<\delta\Rightarrow\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert<\varepsilon.$$

**Check:**

$$\exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall\delta>0\ \exists x:\quad
\lvert x-a\rvert<\delta\ \wedge\ \lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge\varepsilon.$$

Every quantifier flips in place, and $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P\wedge\lnot Q$ — the implication becomes
**and**, not another implication.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Negate $\forall\exists$

Negate:

> For every integer $n>1$, there exists a prime $p$ such that $p$ divides $n$.

**Check:** there exists an integer $n>1$ such that **every** prime $p$ fails to divide $n$:

$$\exists n>1\ \forall p\text{ prime}:\quad p\nmid n.$$

The original is true, so its negation is false. The condition $n>1$ is the **domain**, so it stays fixed:
the negation asks for a counterexample **inside the same domain**, not an unrelated value with $n\le1$.

[for a universal claim, its negation is the statement that a valid counterexample exists]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4+ · Who may depend on whom?

Explain why

$$\forall x\in\mathbb R\ \exists y\in\mathbb R:\ x+y=0$$

is true, while $\exists y\in\mathbb R\ \forall x\in\mathbb R:\ x+y=0$ is false. Then negate both.

**Check:** in the first, choose $y=-x$; in the second, one fixed $y$ cannot work for every $x$.

$$\neg(\forall x\exists y:\ x+y=0)=\exists x\forall y:\ x+y\ne0,$$
$$\neg(\exists y\forall x:\ x+y=0)=\forall y\exists x:\ x+y\ne0.$$

[the later variable may depend on earlier choices; the earlier one cannot depend on later choices]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S5 · One counterexample is enough

A proof claims that the difference between consecutive positive cubes is always prime because

$$(x+1)^3-x^3=3x^2+3x+1$$

and this polynomial is irreducible over the integers. What breaks the proof?

**Check:** irreducible **polynomial** does not mean every integer **value** is prime. At $x=5$ the value is
$91=7\times13$. One counterexample disproves the universal claim.

[algebraic irreducibility $\neq$ numerical primality]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S6 · Start at the hypothesis

The task is to prove $H\Rightarrow C$. A student starts from $C$ and, through correct reversible algebra,
arrives at $H$. What has the written argument proved?

**Check:** as written, it proves the **converse** $C\Rightarrow H$. If every displayed step is explicitly an
equivalence, the chain may be reversed to prove the target — but the argument must say so or run from $H$ to
$C$.

[dedicated clinic: label the first line and last line before checking the middle]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · Where equivalence first fails

A student solving

$$\log_2(3x-1)=1+2\log_2(x-1)$$

replaces $2\log_2(x-1)$ by $\log_2((x-1)^2)$ and later obtains $x=\tfrac12$ or $3$. Where is the first
error if every line claims equivalence?

**Check:** at the replacement. The original requires $x>1$, whereas $\log_2((x-1)^2)$ exists for $x\ne1$.
The widened domain admits the false root $x=\tfrac12$; only $x=3$ solves the original.

[same formula on the old domain; different equation on the larger domain]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

# Part 2 · T1 — Divisors and primes

*Fifteen-plus Paper 2 questions across 2016–2023, and **not one of them a calculation**. The mathematics is
tiny and repeats; learn it cold. Full page: **[T1](../toolkit/t01_divisors_primes.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T1</div>
<div class="fs-title">Divisors &amp; primes — the memorisable core</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Every card has a standard counterexample attached. Learn the counterexample with the fact — that is what the questions actually test.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Primes and the $6n\pm1$ form ★

Every prime $>3$ is of the form $6n\pm1$, because $6n$, $6n\pm2$ and $6n+3$ all carry a factor of $2$ or $3$.

**The converse is false:** $25$, $35$, $49$, $55$ are all $6n\pm1$ and none is prime.

**Edge cases that break proofs:** $1$ is **not** prime; $2$ is the **only** even prime; $3k$ is composite
**only when $k>1$**, since $3\times1=3$ is prime.

[$n^{2}+2$ is prime at $n=1$ — that single case kills several textbook "proofs"]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Euclid's lemma — the missing word ★

**If $p$ divides $ab$, then $p$ divides $a$ or $p$ divides $b$** — *only if $p$ is prime.*

**Drop "prime" and it collapses:** $4$ divides $2\times2$ but $4$ does not divide $2$. Smallest
counterexample $a=4,\ b=c=2$.

[2016 P2 Q13 and 2021 P2 Q4 are the *same* false statement — this is the word they removed]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squaring doubles every exponent ★

$n=p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots\Rightarrow n^{2}=p_1^{2e_1}p_2^{2e_2}\cdots$, so $n^{2}$ carries only **even**
powers.

For a **prime** $p$: if $p$ divides $n^{2}$ then $p$ divides $n$. For a composite divisor you only recover
its square root — **$12$ divides $n^{2}$ exactly when $6$ divides $n$**, *not* when $12$ divides $n$.

**Counterexample:** $n=6$ gives $n^{2}=36=12\times3$, yet $12$ does not divide $6$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Remainders, and what squares leave

"$b$ leaves remainder $r$ on division by $a$" means $b=aq+r$ **with $0\le r<a$** — the size condition is
half the definition.

**Trap:** if $r,s<a$ the product $rs$ need **not** be $<a$, so $rs$ is not the remainder of $bc$. Take
$a=4$, $r=s=2$: $rs=4$, true remainder $0$.

$$n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1,4\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$$

A square is **never** $2\bmod3$ and **never** $3\bmod4$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squares modulo 4 — what a sum of two squares can be ★

Every square is $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$, so

$$a^{2}+b^{2}\equiv 0,\ 1\ 	ext{or}\ 2 \pmod 4 \quad	ext{— never } 3 .$$

**So no integer of the form $4k+3$ is a sum of two squares.** One residue check replaces a search.

Companion facts: a square is never $2mod3$ and never $3mod4$; and modulo $8$ a square is $0$, $1$ or $4$.

[$255=4(63)+3$, so it is not $a^{2}+b^{2}$ — no trial needed]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Digit sums — why the tests work ★

Since $10\equiv1\pmod 9$, every power of $10$ is $\equiv1$, so for the digit sum $s(N)$

$$N\equiv s(N)\pmod 9,\qquad	ext{hence } 9\mid N\iff 9\mid s(N),$$

and the same argument modulo $3$ gives the test for $3$. Modulo $11$, $10\equiv-1$, so the **alternating**
digit sum is what matters.

[$3\mid s(N)$ is necessary but **not** sufficient for $9\mid N$ — take $N=12$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### When does $m\mid n^{k}$ force $m\mid n$? ★

Cubing **triples every exponent** in the prime factorisation, so the condition is about **repeated** primes,
not about being composite:

| $m$ | $m\mid n^{3}\Rightarrow m\mid n$? | |
|---|---|---|
| $2$, $3$, $p$ prime | **yes** | Euclid's lemma |
| $6=2	imes3$ | **yes** | distinct primes, each to the power $1$ |
| $8=2^{3}$ | no | $n=2$ |
| $9=3^{2}$ | no | $n=3$ |

**$m$ works exactly when $m$ is squarefree** — no prime appears twice.

[composite is not the test: $6$ works and $8$ does not]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The gcd toolkit

Let $d=\gcd(a,b)$. This means $d$ is the greatest positive integer dividing **both** $a$ and $b$.
Therefore $a=dr$ and $b=ds$ for some integers $r,s$, so $d$ also divides every integer combination
$xa+yb$ — in particular, $a+b$ and $a-b$.

$$\gcd(a,\,b+ka)=\gcd(a,b)\qquad \gcd(n,\,n+1)=1$$

**Why this matters for a recurrence.** Suppose

$$u_1=a,\qquad u_2=b,\qquad u_{n+2}=u_n+u_{n+1}.$$

If $d$ divides both starting terms, then it divides $u_3=a+b$. It then divides
$u_4=b+u_3$, and the same argument repeats, so $d$ divides **every** term.

Also, the gcd of consecutive terms stays unchanged:

$$\gcd(u_{n+1},u_{n+2})
=\gcd(u_{n+1},u_n+u_{n+1})
=\gcd(u_n,u_{n+1}).$$

[example: $u_1=14,u_2=21$ gives $14,21,35,56,91,\ldots$; every term is divisible by $7$, and each consecutive gcd is $7$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Irreducible $\neq$ prime-valued ★

A polynomial **factorises over the integers** if it can be written as

$$P(x)=A(x)B(x),$$

where $A$ and $B$ are non-constant polynomials whose **every coefficient — including each constant term —
is an integer**. If no such factorisation exists, $P$ is *irreducible over the integers*.

This does **not** mean “it cannot factor over the reals”: for example,
$x^2-2=(x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)$ over the reals, but not over the integers.

Irreducibility describes the polynomial as an algebraic expression; it does not guarantee that the integer
$P(n)$ is prime.

$3x^{2}+3x+1$ is irreducible ($D=9-12=-3<0$), yet $x=5$ gives $91=7\times13$ — which is exactly
$6^{3}-5^{3}$.

In fact, no non-constant polynomial in $\mathbb Z[x]$ gives a prime for **every** integer input. For TMUA,
you do not need the general proof: one composite output is enough to disprove an “always prime” claim.

**Two different meanings of “factor”:** 

- **integer factor:** $91=7\times13$, so $7$ and $13$ divide the number $91$;
- **polynomial factor:** $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ as an identity in $x$.

An irreducible polynomial can therefore produce a composite integer. Treating these two meanings as the
same is the error.
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The two reflexes for this topic

1. **Test $n=1,2,3,4$ before reasoning.** For $n^{3}+5n$ that gives $6,18,42,84$ — one line of arithmetic
   that eliminates five of seven options.
2. **Check the smallest allowed case of every "therefore it is composite" step.** Almost every flawed proof
   in this topic is correct for large $n$ and dies at the boundary.
:::

# Part 3 · T2 — Shapes as logical conditions

*Eight sittings, eight appearances. The geometry never goes beyond GCSE; what is tested is which property
forces which, and whether you can produce the standard counterexample on demand. Full page:
**[T2](../toolkit/t02_shapes_as_logic.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T2</div>
<div class="fs-title">Shapes as logical conditions</div>
<div class="fs-sub">The lattice, the diagonal table, the congruence criteria and the three counterexamples. Learn the <strong>arrows</strong>: every question here is asking you to read one off, usually backwards.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The quadrilateral lattice ★

$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rhombus}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}\Rightarrow\text{trapezium}$$
$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rectangle}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}$$

A square is **both** a rhombus and a rectangle; nothing else is. A **kite** sits outside the chain unless it
is a rhombus.

*Arrows run one way only* — reading one backwards is what every wrong option in this topic does.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The three counterexamples ★

- **rhombus** — equal sides, perpendicular diagonals, **not a square**
- **rectangle** — equal diagonals, right angles, **not a square**
- **isosceles trapezium** — one pair parallel, other pair equal, **not a parallelogram**

Almost every "is this sufficient?" question is killed by one of these three. *Reach for a named shape
before you try to prove anything.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The diagonal table — these are the *iff*s ★

| diagonals | shape guaranteed |
|---|---|
| bisect each other | parallelogram |
| bisect **and equal** | rectangle |
| bisect **and perpendicular** | rhombus |
| bisect, equal **and** perpendicular | square |
| one perpendicularly bisects the other | kite |

Read each as **at least** that shape — a square satisfies every row. Most nec/suff options on the paper are
one of these rows, altered.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Forcing a parallelogram

**Sufficient, each alone:** both pairs of sides parallel · both pairs equal · the **same one pair** both
equal **and** parallel · diagonals bisect each other.

**Not sufficient — the exam's favourite:** one pair *equal* and a **different** pair *parallel*
($AB=CD$ but $AD\parallel BC$). That describes an **isosceles trapezium**.

*Splitting "equal" and "parallel" across different pairs is the whole trap.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Congruence, and the one that is not ★

**Criteria:** SSS · SAS · ASA · AAS · RHS.

**SSA is not a criterion** — two sides and a *non-included* angle give the ambiguous case, two triangles.

**Equal area is not a criterion either:** $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ equal gives only $\sin C_1=\sin C_2$, and

$$\sin A=\sin B\iff B=A\ \text{ or }\ B=180^\circ-A .$$

*Whenever an angle is recovered from a sine, stop — there are two possibilities.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The midpoint quadrilateral ★

Join the midpoints of the sides of **any** quadrilateral: the result is **always a parallelogram**, with its
sides parallel to the diagonals and half their length.

| condition on the diagonals of $ABCD$ | midpoint quadrilateral |
|---|---|
| none | parallelogram |
| equal | **rhombus** |
| perpendicular | **rectangle** |
| equal **and** perpendicular | **square** |

*Each row is an **iff**, so this converts a fact about the diagonals into one about the sides and back.*

[equal gives the rhombus, perpendicular gives the rectangle — not the other way round]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Polygons and circles

$$\text{interior sum}=(n-2)\times180^\circ\qquad\text{regular interior}=180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

$n=3,4,5,6,8,12\Rightarrow60^\circ,90^\circ,108^\circ,120^\circ,135^\circ,150^\circ$.

**Pentagon consequence:** five angles in arithmetic progression sum to $5a=540^\circ$, so the **middle one
is forced to be $108^\circ$**, whatever the common difference.

**Equal areas from the centre $\neq$ regular:** each central angle is $\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$, so
only $n=3$ forces regularity. For $n=4$, angles $60,120,60,120$ work.

**Cyclic quadrilateral:** opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ — a genuine *iff*.
:::

::::

:::::

---

# Part 4 · The recurring mathematical engines

*Paper 2 recombines a short reasoning list with ordinary Paper 1 mathematics. The cards below are not a
second Paper 1 formula sheet: they are the moves that repeatedly decide the reasoning questions.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Applications and reasoning</div>
<div class="fs-title">Eight engines that carry the logic</div>
<div class="fs-sub">For each one: remember the fact, recognise the question shape, then use the routine.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Roots and graphs ★

**Formula / facts**

$$f(x)=0\iff\text{$x$-intercept},\qquad f'(x)=0\iff\text{stationary point}.$$

A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ real roots. Between two distinct roots of differentiable $f$ lies
a root of $f'$ (Rolle), so $n$ distinct roots of $f$ force at least $n-1$ roots of $f'$.

**Never reverse it:** a stationary point need not give two roots. $f(x)=x^2+1$ has $f'(0)=0$ but no real
root.

**Frequent type — “how many roots are possible?”** Sketch the simplest allowed shape; count intersections,
not algebraic solutions. Use end behaviour + turning points + tangencies. A repeated root touches; a simple
root crosses.

[example: $x|x|=px+q$ means intersect the two-branch graph $y=x|x|$ with a line]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Calculus conditions ★

**Formula / facts**

$$f'(a)=0\text{ is necessary, not sufficient, for an interior differentiable maximum/minimum.}$$
$$f''(a)>0\Rightarrow\text{local minimum},\qquad f''(a)<0\Rightarrow\text{local maximum}.$$

$f''(a)=0$ alone proves nothing: $x^4$ has a minimum at $0$; $x^3$ has an inflection there.
An inflection needs **concavity to change sign**. Increasing means $f'\ge0$ (strictly increasing does not
require $f'>0$ at every point: $x^3$ is the standard counterexample).

**Frequent type — necessary or sufficient?** Translate the geometric word into its exact derivative
condition, then test both arrows with $x^2$, $x^3$, $x^4$ or a constant function.

[memory: stationary = flat; turning = changes direction; inflection = changes bend]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Inequalities and domains ★

**Safe moves:** add the same expression; multiply by a known positive number; square only after controlling
signs. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign.

$$a^2\ge0,\qquad (a-b)^2\ge0\Rightarrow a^2+b^2\ge2ab,$$
$$\sqrt{X}=|Y|\text{ when }X=Y^2,\qquad \cos x=\pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2x}.$$

**Domains:** denominators $\ne0$; square-root inputs $\ge0$; logarithm inputs $>0$. For $0<a<1$,
$\log_a x$ is decreasing, so an inequality reverses when applying it.

**Frequent type — first error.** Annotate every risky line with its missing condition: “divisor non-zero?”,
“both sides non-negative?”, “log base above 1?”, “domain retained?”. Stop at the first missing condition.

[counterexample to multiplying inequalities: $-3<-2$ and $-1<0$, but $3\not<0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Transformations and solution counts

Horizontal shifts, reflections and non-zero stretches preserve the **number** of roots:

$$f(x-a)=0,\quad f(-x)=0,\quad f(kx)=0\ (k\ne0)$$

are re-labellings of the roots of $f$. A vertical shift $f(x)+c=0$ can change the count.

Inverse graphs reflect in $y=x$, so $f(x)=x$ and $f^{-1}(x)=x$ have the same fixed points (when the inverse
exists). But squaring or modulus can add a branch:

$$|f(x)|=k\iff f(x)=\pm k\qquad(k\ge0).$$

**Frequent type — “same number of solutions”.** Substitute to expose a bijection between solution sets.
If the manipulation introduces $\pm$, squares, or discards a domain, count the new branches separately.

[example: $\cos^2x=c^2$ means $\cos x=c$ or $\cos x=-c$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Trigonometric counting ★

$$\sin u=\sin\alpha\Rightarrow u=\alpha+360^\circ k\text{ or }180^\circ-\alpha+360^\circ k,$$
$$\cos u=\cos\alpha\Rightarrow u=\pm\alpha+360^\circ k.$$

For $u=mx+c$, **transform the interval first**, solve in $u$, then convert back. Endpoints matter.

**Frequent type — number of solutions / sufficient condition.** Draw one-period graphs and count horizontal
line intersections. Split squares or modulus into $+$ and $-$ levels before counting.

**Two traps:** $\sin A=\sin B$ does not force $A=B$; and $\sqrt{\cos^2x}=|\cos x|$, not $\cos x$.

[memory: equation in $2x$ over $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ spans two full turns]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Sequences, invariants and pigeonholes

For a recurrence, calculate only enough terms to guess what cannot change: parity, remainder, sign, gcd, or
a bounded range. Then prove that property survives one recurrence step.

$$\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a+kb),\qquad \text{consecutive recurrence terms often carry the same gcd.}$$

**Pigeonhole principle:** putting $N$ objects into $k$ boxes forces some box to contain at least
$\lceil N/k\rceil$ objects. For “must occur”, choose boxes so one overfull box is exactly the desired pair.

**Frequent type — which must be true?** Search for an invariant before testing long lists. For a claimed
possibility, build one short example; for a necessity, try extremes and equality cases first.

[example: residues mod $m$ are the $m$ boxes; $m+1$ integers force two equal residues]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Integrals without full calculation

$$\int_a^b(f(x)+c)\,dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+c(b-a),$$
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\!f(x)\,dx=0\text{ if $f$ is odd},\qquad
\int_{-a}^{a}\!f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^a\!f(x)\,dx\text{ if $f$ is even}.$$

If $f\le g$ throughout $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f\le\int_a^b g$. An integral is **signed area**: below
the axis contributes negatively.

**Frequent type — compare / infer without integrating.** Simplify the integrand first; look for symmetry,
a constant vertical shift, or a pointwise inequality. For $f(|x|)$, mirror the right half; split at $0$.

[example: replacing $f$ by $f+C$ adds the rectangle $C(b-a)$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Lines and circles as conditions

For $ax+by=c$ ($a,b\ne0$):

$$m=-\frac ab,\qquad x\text{-intercept}=\frac ca,\qquad y\text{-intercept}=\frac cb.$$

Perpendicular lines satisfy $m_1m_2=-1$. A circle tangent to an axis has
**distance from centre to the axis = radius**.

**Frequent type — necessary/sufficient data.** Convert each geometric statement to one algebraic equation,
then ask whether it determines the target uniquely. If free variables remain, it is not sufficient.

**Cyclic invariant:** for gradients $-a/b,-b/c,-c/a$, the product is $-1$ — simplify the whole cycle
before testing cases.

[sign trap: positive gradient tells the signs of $a,b$ are opposite, but not the sign of $c$]{.eg}
:::

::::

:::::

# Part 5 · The exam-day card

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you read a single question

Write these at the top of your rough paper:

1. $\;$ **sufficient $\to$ forwards, necessary $\to$ backwards**
2. $\;$ **contrapositive = equivalent; converse = trap**
3. $\;$ $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P$ **and** $\lnot Q$
4. $\;$ **rhombus · rectangle · isosceles trapezium** — the three counterexamples
5. $\;$ $p$ divides $ab$ $\Rightarrow$ $p$ divides $a$ or $p$ divides $b$ — **only for prime $p$**
6. $\;$ $\sqrt{u^2}=|u|$ · $f'(a)=0$ is not automatically a turn · check every domain
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thirty-second routine for any Paper 2 question

**Name the reasoning type first, then do the mathematics.** Almost every lost mark comes from competent
mathematics done on the wrong question.

| The question says… | It is asking for… | So you… |
|---|---|---|
| "necessary", "sufficient" | set inclusion | find the **exact** set, then compare |
| "must be true" | $\forall$ | find a counterexample, or prove it |
| "possible", "can" | $\exists$ | **produce one witness** |
| "which is equivalent" | contrapositive | negate both halves and reverse |
| "first error", "best describes" | Err1/Err2 | read down, stop at the first failure |
| "number of solutions" | intersections | sketch, transform the interval, count branches |
| "same number of roots" | bijection | substitute; watch for $\pm$, squaring and domains |
| recurrence / long list | invariant | test parity, remainder, sign, gcd, bounds |
| no logical wording at all | Paper 1 technique | just calculate — about a quarter of the paper |
:::
